newsitem.title: USA: Washington state to hold onto tobacco stocks.
newsitem.headline: Washington state to hold onto tobacco stocks.

text.p: The board that oversees Washington state's $39.5 billion pension system defeated a motion Thursday that called for it to divest the state's holdings in tobacco stocks.

Last month, the board's public markets committee unanimously recommended that Washington state dump its tobacco holdings, but since then state attorneys general have announced a proposed settlement with the industry.
"It does appear some of the cloud of uncertainty over the industry has been lifted. I'm not sure I would divest anymore," said money manager Paula Treneer, who participated in the board's debate.
The Washington state Investment Board deadlocked 4-4 on the motion to divest about $226 million in tobacco-related stocks, effectively defeating the proposal.
Board members said they do not anticipate returning to the issue this year. Tobacco securities represent less than 1 percent of the total pension investments.

By law, board members are charged with maximizing the return to the state's retirees. The Investment Board is not allowed to take social goals into consideration. About 434,000 teachers, state workers and retirees have money invested in state pension funds.
Board Vice Chair George Masten said he pressed for divestment purely on financial grounds.
"The tobacco industry is under major assault," Masten argued. "I don't think this is going to stop. In fact, I think this is going to get even more volatile."
"There are other opportunities out there that will probably provide better returns," added fellow board member Gary Moore.

Other board members countered that Wall Street had already factored the downside risk to tobacco into stock prices. They also argued against setting a precedent by freezing out a specific industry beset by bad news.
